info.title: Nocturne.API | nightscout
info.description:
The legacy Nightscout REST API (v1–v3), preserved for **1:1 compatibility** with the original JavaScript implementation.

Every legacy write decomposes into Nocturne's granular v4 domain models, and every read projects back from v4 into the legacy shape — there are no standalone legacy tables. See the **Data Model** section for how each legacy collection (entries, treatments, devicestatus, profiles) maps to v4.

place and projecting the result back.

get.description:
On error, returns the same envelope with the app version and an unknown storage version to maintain
compatibility with clients that depend on this endpoint always returning 200.

The access token in the URL is the caller's only credential — this is the bootstrap
that exchanges it for a JWT (used by NSClientV3/AAPS). It must be anonymous: the
class-level `[Authorize]` would otherwise reject the request with 401 before the
method can validate the token. The action validates the token itself and returns 401
when it is missing or invalid.

Accepts both legacy subject access tokens (`name-hexstring`, resolved against
subjects) and `noc_` direct-grant tokens (resolved against oauth_grants; the
minted JWT carries the grant's scopes and tenant pin).

get.description:
Like Nightscout, `find[...]` filters narrow the result, a find that bounds neither
`created_at` nor `dateString` reads only the last four days, and the result is
unlimited unless count is given, up to the merged read cap.
The scope requirement is an OR because the response merges four storages, each with its own
read scope. Admission means the caller holds at least one of those categories;
ActivityReadScopeGuard then removes the records whose category the caller does
not hold. Pagination is applied by the service before the filter, so a caller holding a
subset of the categories can receive fewer than count records.

get.description:
The scope requirement is an OR over the four storages this route resolves against, and
ActivityReadScopeGuard then checks the resolved record's own category. A record
in a category the caller does not hold answers 404 rather than 403, so the response does not
disclose that the record exists.

get.description:
`CountActivitiesAsync` sums four storages — StateSpans, heart rates, step counts and
sleep sessions — into a single number, so unlike the record-returning activity endpoints
the result cannot be filtered down to the categories the caller holds. The requirement is
therefore every category's read scope (AND), which is what the legacy admin, `api:*:read`
and `readable` grants carry. Serving a per-category count needs a source-aware count on
`IActivityService`.

collection the route serves and would let a grant scoped to one category learn a row count
for another. `activity` merges four categories and keeps the AND below.

tags.name: ns-model-devicestatus
tags.description:
How legacy **devicestatus** maps to Nocturne's v4 device model. A Nightscout devicestatus document bundles several independent status objects (`openaps`/`loop`, `pump`, `uploader`) into one blob. Nocturne decomposes it into separate v4 snapshots — **ApsSnapshot**, **PumpSnapshot**, and **UploaderSnapshot** — sharing a `CorrelationId` so the original document can be reassembled on read. Keeping them separate lets each evolve and be queried on its own. ## Data Model **V1 DeviceStatus Decomposition** _How the legacy DeviceStatus blob (with nested openaps/loop/pump/uploader status objects) is decomposed into ApsSnapshot, PumpSnapshot, and UploaderSnapshot rows sharing a CorrelationId, and why each is separate._ ```mermaid --- title: "V1 DeviceStatus Decomposition" --- flowchart LR subgraph legacy["V1 Monolithic DeviceStatus"] direction TB device["device, mills, utcOffset"] subgraph blob["Nested status objects (single document)"] direction TB openaps["openaps (suggested, enacted, iob, cob, predBGs, version)"] loop["loop (iob, cob, predicted, recommendedBolus, enacted)"] pump["pump (reservoir, battery, status, iob, manufacturer, model, clock)"] uploader["uploader (battery, voltage, name, type, temperature)"] xdrip["xdripjs, radioAdapter, cgm, meter, override, insulinPen, mmtune, ..."] end end openaps --> ApsSnapshot loop --> ApsSnapshot pump --> PumpSnapshot uploader --> UploaderSnapshot xdrip -. extras .-> ApsSnapshot xdrip -. extras .-> PumpSnapshot xdrip -. extras .-> UploaderSnapshot subgraph v4["V4 Decomposed Snapshots (share CorrelationId)"] direction TB ApsSnapshot["ApsSnapshot
aidAlgorithm iob, basalIob, bolusIob, cob currentBg, eventualBg, targetBg recommendedBolus, sensitivityRatio enacted, enactedRate, enactedDuration enactedBolusVolume predictedDefault/Iob/Zt/Cob/UamJson predictedStartTimestamp suggestedJson, enactedJson, loopJson"] PumpSnapshot["PumpSnapshot
manufacturer, model reservoir, reservoirDisplay batteryPercent, batteryVoltage bolusing, suspended, pumpStatus clock, iob, bolusIob deviceId (FK)"] UploaderSnapshot["UploaderSnapshot
name, type battery, batteryVoltage isCharging, temperature deviceId (FK)"] end subgraph reasons["Why Decompose?"] direction TB r1["Different update cadences
An APS algorithm runs every 5 minutes. Pump reservoir level only changes after a bolus. Phone battery shifts on its own schedule. Bundling them forces three writes when only one concern moved."] r2["Different consumers
The 'is my Loop running?' monitor only cares about ApsSnapshot. The 'reservoir low' alert only cares about PumpSnapshot. Decomposition lets each subscriber query just what it needs."] r3["Different identity scopes
Pump and uploader belong to physical hardware (FK to Device). An APS algorithm decision is tied to software, not hardware -- the same pump can run different algorithms over time."] r4["Different retention needs
APS snapshots are the audit trail for algorithm decisions and need long retention. Pump/uploader battery telemetry can be downsampled aggressively once the live state is captured."] r5["Schema clarity
The legacy blob mixes 8+ vendor-specific shapes (openaps, loop, xdripjs, mmtune, etc.). Typed V4 records normalize OpenAPS/AAPS/Loop into a single ApsSnapshot with raw blobs preserved for round-trip."] r6["Decomposition idempotency
One legacy DeviceStatus produces up to 3 V4 records sharing one CorrelationId. Re-running decomposition updates the same three rows rather than duplicating data."] end ApsSnapshot -.- r1 PumpSnapshot -.- r1 UploaderSnapshot -.- r1 v4 -.- r2 PumpSnapshot -.- r3 ApsSnapshot -.- r4 v4 -.- r5 v4 -.- r6 ```

tags.name: ns-model-entries
tags.description:
How legacy **entries** map to Nocturne's v4 glucose model. A Nightscout entry is a single polymorphic document discriminated by `type` (`sgv`, `mbg`, `cal`). Nocturne does not store entries as one table — on write each entry is routed by type into a dedicated v4 glucose table, and reads project those tables back into the legacy entry shape. | Legacy entry `type` | Nocturne v4 model | | --- | --- | | `sgv` (sensor glucose) | **SensorGlucose** | | `mbg` (meter blood glucose) | **MeterGlucose** / **BGCheck** | | `cal` (calibration) | **Calibration** | Splitting by source preserves each reading's true units, fidelity, provenance, and device linkage rather than flattening everything into one numeric blob. ## Data Model **Glucose Source Taxonomy** _Why SensorGlucose, MeterGlucose, BGCheck, and Calibration are four separate tables. Different source-of-truth units, fidelity, provenance, retention, and device linkage._ ```mermaid --- title: "Glucose Source Taxonomy" --- flowchart LR subgraph sources["Where glucose values come from"] direction TB cgm["CGM stream
(Dexcom, Libre, Guardian, etc.)"] meterAuto["Connected meter
(auto-uploaded via connector / xDrip)"] meterManual["User-typed BG
(treatment context: 'I just checked, 6.2')"] oldCgm["Legacy CGM

tags.name: ns-model-profile
tags.description:
How legacy **profiles** map to Nocturne's v4 therapy model. A Nightscout profile is a monolithic document holding therapy settings plus four time-of-day schedules. Nocturne decomposes it into granular v4 models — **Therapy Settings** and separate **Basal**, **Carb Ratio**, **Sensitivity**, and **Target Range** schedules — so each can be versioned and validated independently. Reads project them back into the single legacy profile shape. ## Data Model **V1 Profile Decomposition** _How the monolithic Nightscout v1 profile is decomposed into granular v4 domain models, and why each separation exists._ ```mermaid --- title: "V1 Profile Decomposition" --- flowchart LR subgraph legacy["V1 Monolithic Profile"] direction TB store["store[name]"] subgraph blob["ProfileData (single JSON blob)"] direction TB dia["dia, carbs_hr, delay
GI variants"] tz["timezone, units
perGIvalues"] basal["basal[]"] carbratio["carbratio[]"] sens["sens[]"] target_low["target_low[]"] target_high["target_high[]"] end meta["defaultProfile
enteredBy
startDate"] loop["loopSettings
deviceToken, dosingStrategy
override presets, guards"] end dia --> TherapySettings tz --> TherapySettings meta --> TherapySettings loop --> TherapySettings basal --> BasalSchedule carbratio --> CarbRatioSchedule sens --> SensitivitySchedule target_low --> TargetRangeSchedule target_high --> TargetRangeSchedule subgraph v4["V4 Decomposed Models"] direction TB TherapySettings["TherapySettings

dia, carbsHr, delay, GI variants timezone, units, perGIValues loopSettings, enteredBy isDefault, startDate"] BasalSchedule["BasalSchedule

time-of-day insulin delivery rates (U/hr)"] CarbRatioSchedule["CarbRatioSchedule

time-of-day insulin-to-carb ratios (g/U)"] SensitivitySchedule["SensitivitySchedule

time-of-day insulin sensitivity factors"] TargetRangeSchedule["TargetRangeSchedule

merged low + high into time-of-day target ranges"] end subgraph reasons["Why Decompose?"] direction TB r1["Pharmacokinetics vs preferences

DIA and carb absorption are drug properties; timezone and units are user display preferences. Bundling them forces a full profile push when only one concern changes."] r2["Independent schedule lifecycles

Basal rates change when a pump is adjusted. Carb ratios change when diet shifts. ISF changes with activity patterns. Coupling them means every tweak overwrites the entire profile."] r3["Target ranges are clinical policy

Target ranges are set by endocrinologists and change on clinic visits. They should not be bundled with self-adjusted basal rates or carb ratios."] r4["Audit granularity

With a monolith, 'profile updated' tells you nothing. Decomposed records show exactly which parameter changed, when, and by which device or app."] r5["Query efficiency

A connector fetching basal rates for pump sync should not load carb ratios, sensitivity factors, and Loop device tokens."] r6["Loop settings are device config

Device tokens, dosing strategies, and override presets are APS integration concerns, not therapy parameters. Mixing them means
a Loop settings sync can
overwrite clinical therapy data."] end TherapySettings -.- r1 TherapySettings -.- r6 BasalSchedule -.- r2 CarbRatioSchedule -.- r2 SensitivitySchedule -.- r2 TargetRangeSchedule -.- r3 v4 -.- r4 v4 -.- r5 ```

tags.name: ns-model-treatments
tags.description:
How legacy **treatments** map to Nocturne's v4 treatment model. A Nightscout treatment is a single polymorphic blob whose `eventType` determines which fields are meaningful. On write, Nocturne routes each treatment by `eventType` into focused v4 domain models (boluses, carb intakes, temp basals, BG checks, notes, site/sensor changes, …); sibling rows that originated from one treatment stay linked by a shared `CorrelationId`. Reads recombine those rows back into the legacy treatment shape. ## Data Model **V1 Treatment Decomposition** _How the polymorphic v1 treatment blob is decomposed into focused v4 domain models based on eventType routing._ ```mermaid --- title: "V1 Treatment Decomposition" --- flowchart LR subgraph legacy["V1 Monolithic Treatment"] direction TB et["eventType (string)

→ Bolus + CarbIntake"] m2["Correction Bolus

Insulin on board depends only on
boluses and pharmacokinetics.
Carbs on board depends only on
intake and absorption time.
Bundling them conflates two
independent calculation domains."] r2["Measurements are not actions
A finger-stick BG check is an
observation, not a treatment.
Grouping it with insulin delivery
corrupts 'show me all treatments'
queries with passive readings."] r3["Decisions vs delivery
A bolus calculator captures why
a dose was chosen. The bolus
itself captures what was delivered.
Not every calculation produces a
bolus; not every bolus comes from
a calculator. Separating them
enables decision-chain auditing."] r4["Point events vs time spans
Boluses are instantaneous.
Temp basals and profile switches
are active for a duration.
They need start/end timestamps
and state-tracking infrastructure
that point-event models lack."] r5["Freeform text vs structured data
Notes are annotations on the
timeline. Any record can carry
notes (bolus, device event, etc.)
Separating them avoids bloating
every model with a notes field
and lets notes exist standalone."] r6["Device lifecycle vs clinical events
Site changes, sensor starts,
and pod changes are hardware
maintenance, not clinical therapy.
A strongly-typed enum replaces
fragile string matching and
enables 'last site change?' queries."] r7["Polymorphic blob prevents type safety
One class with ~100 nullable fields
means any field can appear on any
record. Decomposed models enforce
which fields belong where at the
schema level, not by convention."] r8["APS algorithm vs manual actions
SMBs from AAPS and auto-boluses
from Loop are fundamentally
different from manual corrections.
Bolus.Kind (Algorithm vs Manual)
and Automatic flag distinguish
them for safety analysis."] end Bolus -.- r1 CarbIntake -.- r1 BGCheck -.- r2 BolusCalc -.- r3 TempBasal -.- r4 StateSpan -.- r4 Note -.- r5 DeviceEvent -.- r6 v4 -.- r7 Bolus -.- r8 ```

tags.name: V1
tags.description:
Legacy Nightscout V1 API — **1:1 compatible** with the original JavaScript implementation.

Covers the core Nightscout data model: entries (SGV, MBG, CAL), treatments (bolus, temp basal, carb corrections, site changes), profiles, device status, and food records. Also includes Alexa voice assistant integration and Pebble smartwatch endpoints.

All writes decompose into V4 granular models — there are no standalone legacy tables. Reads project back from V4 data into the legacy shape.

> **Timestamps:** V1 uses a "mills-first" convention. Clients that write entries must provide `date` in epoch milliseconds.

> **Authentication:** V1 endpoints accept the legacy `api_secret` header (SHA-1 hash) or token-based auth via `?token=` query parameter. Both are supported for backwards compatibility.

tags.name: V2
tags.description:
Enhanced Nightscout V2 API — maintains compatibility with legacy V2 consumers.

- **Authorization** — Token permission checking.
- **DData** — Direct data access for aggregated reads.
- **Loop** — Apple Push Notification Service (APNS) integration for the iOS Loop app.
- **Notifications** — Enhanced notification system with push support.
- **Properties** — Client properties and runtime settings.
- **Summary** — Aggregated data endpoints for dashboard widgets.

tags.name: V3
tags.description:
Nightscout V3 RESTful API — full CRUD with `Last-Modified` / `If-Modified-Since` support.

Provides a consistent RESTful interface across all core collections: entries, treatments, device status, food, profiles, and settings. Each collection supports filtering, pagination, field projection, and soft-delete semantics. All writes decompose into V4 granular models — reads project back from V4 data into the legacy shape.

- **Last Modified** — Timestamps for when each collection was last modified, enabling efficient polling via conditional requests.
- **Status** — Extended status with permissions and authorization details.
- **Version** — Server version information.

> **Note:** V3 uses `identifier` (a string field) as the primary key for records, not the MongoDB `_id`. When migrating from V1, ensure your client uses the correct identifier field.
